text: If Cassini just ran out of fuel, it would eventually drift somewhere in the Saturn system, and any Earth microbes it carried could land on a moon. That’s the worry, and it’s especially serious for Enceladus, since it has an ocean under its ice. So NASA planned the last orbit to be low and short, then aimed the spacecraft directly into Saturn’s atmosphere. The crash wasn’t an accident; it was the intended final move, and the planet’s gravity was doing most of the work, with just enough fuel to guide the last pass into the atmosphere.

That hurts because your body is absorbing forces your leg isn't built to take in that posture. When you're on a skateboard, even if one leg looks planted, the whole body is still moving. Your foot has to keep grip on the deck, the knee bends and straightens under impact, and the hip takes the shock from each turn or wheel hit. If you're riding on rough ground, that strain gets much worse because every bump goes right through your leg. You may also be overusing your push leg or holding a fixed position for too long, which can leave the muscles tired and aching after you stop.

If it's the back leg, that's the one doing most of the work getting you moving. It's natural to feel it after a session. Aches in the hip, thigh, or calf can come from the repeated push-off motion and landing. The knee might also complain if you're going down slopes, since the joint is absorbing impact. If the pain is just a dull ache after skating, that's typical muscle fatigue. If it's sharp or comes back immediately, pay attention to whether it's in a joint or a muscle.

A lot of skaters get pain because they skate through it for a while. You don't have to be a pro to feel it; beginners get it too, because the muscles and joints are learning how to handle the impact. Stretching the leg after a ride helps with stiffness, but it won't fix everything. If the pain lingers or gets worse, that's a sign to check your form. Are you landing too hard or holding your legs too stiff? Softening your knees a little lets your body absorb force better. Also, check that your board isn't too loose, and make sure your shoes have enough grip on the deck. Those small changes can take pressure off your leg.

The short of it: your stationary leg hurts because it's not actually stationary. It's taking the impact, the turning, and the landing. If it hurts, back off a bit, stretch, and look at how you're landing.

yeah that's a fair point, and I'd say it's mostly about ancestry and identity, not actual geography. "Afro-" refers to African roots, even if the person grew up in Ohio or Texas and has never been to Africa. A lot of Black Americans trace their families back through the transatlantic slave trade, especially from places like West Africa, so the label is a way of connecting people to that shared history rather than saying everyone there is a current resident of Africa.

I think the term also overlaps with other "Afro-" identities, like Afro-Asian or Afro-Latinx, which can blur the lines. If you're asking about the US specifically, it's less about citizenship and more about cultural identity and where a person's ancestors came from.

at least that's how I'd understand it. if the label feels off to you, you're not the only one.

I think part of the confusion is that "bad" is being used as a blanket label, when really each substance has its own profile of benefits, risks, and side effects. People don't want the euphoria without a cost, but cost is not optional. A drug can be very pleasurable and still produce tolerance. That's one of the big problems. Your brain adapts, and what was a huge high becomes a normal baseline, so you need more to get the same feeling. That's not a rare exception, it's how reward systems work for a lot of things.

You also don't need the drug to be "bad" in the cultural sense for adverse effects to exist. Sleep changes, appetite changes, heart rate changes, mood swings, dependence risk. Even if a substance is safer than others, zero adverse effects is a very strong claim. In practice, almost anything you put into your body that changes how it feels will shift your brain chemistry in some way. And the way a drug feels at first is not how it feels after repeated use.

There's also the difference between the drug and the way people use it. Dose, timing, setting, and how often someone takes it matter a lot. A substance that feels mild once a week might feel quite different if someone takes it every night. So "all drugs are bad" is an oversimplification, but "no adverse effects" is also a lot to ask for.

Could a perfectly pleasant, zero-cost euphoric exist? Maybe in theory, but the pleasure itself is a kind of effect. The brain learns the drug, and that learning is an adverse effect in the sense that you're now dependent on the stimulus to feel normal. That's the part that's hard to avoid.

That silk test is actually used as a quick warning sign for a stroke. The "5" and "spell silk" part is checking word processing and coordination. Cows drinking milk is a simple logic trap. If you get caught by that little trick, it can point to attention or language issues, and with the silk test that's worth taking seriously. I don't know for sure what's going on, but at least that's how it was explained to me. The important thing is getting checked, not just guessing.

Have your brother ask a doctor about the results, or maybe a neurologist. Better safe than sorry.

Hi Sam,

3-in-1 isn't one product that does three jobs, it's a compromise mix. Shampoos lean on sulfates to strip oil and dirt, while conditioners lean on silicones and fatty alcohols to coat and soften. The 3-in-1 has to balance those opposing needs, so it usually ends up with a milder detergent base and lighter conditioning agents than a standalone shampoo or conditioner. On top of that, a bodywash formula is made for skin, not scalp hair, so the 3-in-1 is typically tuned to be gentle enough for both surfaces.

A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner usually just mixes surfactants with conditioners in one bottle. With three jobs, you lose specificity: it cleans well enough for body and scalp, but doesn't condition hair as deeply as a dedicated conditioner. That's where the difference shows, and it really depends on how much hair you're dealing with. Are you using it on wet or dry hair?

So basically they use this thing called GPS. Like actual GPS satellites that track specific points on the ground. If you stick a GPS receiver on a rock in a mountain range, it can track its position over years, and that tells you how fast the plate is moving. They also use this stuff called InSAR, which is satellite radar that measures tiny ground movement, stuff like a few centimeters per year. Another big one is seismic data, from analyzing earthquake waves. And there's paleomagnetic stuff too, from rocks. It's not like they just guess. The rates are pretty small, like a few centimeters per year, so it takes a long time to get good data. Also, they compare the current movement to the direction of the plate boundary, which helps confirm the model. And the whole thing gets cross-checked with other methods so it's not just one data source.
Cheers

When related parents have children, they're more likely to share the same ancestors and therefore the same recessive variants. A child of two related people has a higher chance of inheriting the same variant from both parents, making them homozygous (two identical copies). If the variant is harmful, two copies can be expressed in the child. Most harmful variants affecting the brain are recessive, so they stay hidden when a person has only one copy.

IQ is influenced by hundreds of genes. Inbreeding increases the chance that hidden mutations get expressed, and it also reduces genetic diversity, a problem called inbreeding depression. The result can be lower cognitive scores. Most of these variants have small effects, and a child of inbred parents may inherit several at once, which together can drag IQ scores down. That's why it shows up as a population-level difference rather than a guarantee for every child.

The short version is that the arm is mostly skin, muscle, and a few major nerves, so the same injury there often feels less shocking than a hit to the chest or leg. The body’s central nervous system is more sensitive to danger signals, so a punch to the stomach can feel worse than the same blow to the forearm.

Also, the arm’s nerves carry a lot of everyday pressure, so they’re more used to being stretched or pressed. A shot to the arm might feel more like a sharp thud or vibration before the pain builds up. In your house or office, if someone gets hit in the arm, that initial “surprise” effect is usually smaller.

So it isn’t that your arm is tougher everywhere; it’s that the core is more defended. I could be wrong about the exact threshold differences, but that’s how it was explained to me. If it stings less, you’re likely fine for a bit.

Your body produces carbon dioxide as a normal byproduct of metabolism, and you constantly breathe it out. It's a natural part of the carbon cycle, and your lungs easily exchange it with oxygen from the air. You can breathe in moderate amounts of CO2 without dying, which is why being in a crowded room or a greenhouse isn't instantly lethal.

Carbon monoxide is a different story. It's a colorless, odorless gas that gets into your blood and attaches to the hemoglobin in your red blood cells. It grabs onto that hemoglobin about 200 to 250 times tighter than oxygen does. This leaves almost no room for oxygen to bind, starving your organs of the fuel they need. Your brain and heart are especially vulnerable. It's a deadly trap.

Why doesn't CO2 do the same thing? It doesn't have that extreme affinity for hemoglobin. Instead, it simply diffuses out through your lungs. The danger with CO2 is mainly if you breathe in a massive amount, like being trapped in a sealed basement (a scenario we deal with in the facilities team). But CO will quietly steal your oxygen at much lower concentrations.

Consider a car parked in a garage with the engine running. The exhaust is full of CO. You might not notice it building up until you're feeling dizzy or getting a headache. That's your body warning you that oxygen isn't reaching your brain. If you work around combustion equipment or manage facilities, keeping the ventilation moving and checking the exhaust systems is your best defense.

When a plane stops abruptly, your body keeps moving. That forward momentum is what causes most of the severe injuries, like your head slamming into the seatback or your organs shifting. The brace position is a way to lock your body into a compact shape. It forces you to take the impact on your muscles and bones, which are much stronger than your internal organs. It keeps your body from breaking apart.

You pull your knees up to your chest, and hold your head down and forward (this stops the neck from whiplash). Does that mean you'll survive a crash? It won't guarantee that, but it changes how your body absorbs the shock. You're kinda using your strongest muscles as a shock absorber instead of letting your spine and organs take the brunt of the hit. It also stops your legs from kicking the person in front of you so they don't take extra impact.

Cabin crews demonstrate this exact move during preflight checks. You just follow their lead. If the seatbelt is tight against your hips and your knees are up, you're ready for the worst.

Most recognizable brands are tied to the industrial era because that's when companies started producing large quantities of standardized goods and building mass-market name recognition. Before that, trade was much more local and workshop-based. Firms could be successful in their own neighborhoods, but they rarely became famous beyond their immediate area. Industrialization brought factories, distribution networks, and wider advertising, which made company names spread far beyond one place. That's why the big household names we know tend to come from that later period, rather than from pre-industrial businesses.

People get tripped up by the sticker on the window and the bank quote. I’m not one to say the dealer is always a ripoff, but I think the advertised low rate is a trap unless you look at the whole bill. A bank might offer 4% while the dealer offers 3%, yet the dealer can still cost you more if they bundle an extended warranty or service plan you don’t need.

I remember reading that dealerships are often paid by the manufacturer to use their in-house finance arm, and that’s where the hidden costs live. The low rate is the bait. You think you’re saving, but then the total amount financed is padded with extras. The bank’s higher rate is applied to a cleaner loan with fewer add-ons.

I’m not a car finance expert, but at least that’s how I understand it. I’d never take the dealer’s 3% if the contract includes a 20,000 mile extended warranty and a $400 service plan. I’d rather take the bank’s 4% on the actual vehicle price. That’s how I’d play it, though I could be wrong.

Here’s what I’d actually do. I’d get the bank’s full quote, including the APR, term, and monthly payment. Then I’d get the dealer’s itemized contract. Not just the rate, but every line item. If the dealer’s total interest over the loan term is higher, the lower rate means nothing. I’d even ask the bank if they’d match or beat the dealer’s rate once the extras are on the table. Sometimes they will.

The core idea isn’t about the number on the sign. It’s about the total cost of the loan. That’s where the real comparison happens.

Marijuana is legal in some states and not in others, and that split is the whole problem. You can buy cannabis at a shop in New Mexico or California, but cross the line and it might be a crime in the next state over. That inconsistency feels backwards to me. It's one of the same molecules.

I think the country needs to stop treating it like a patchwork quilt of rules. If a state legalizes it for personal use, at least let people keep using it without a lawyer. There are states like New Mexico that let you use it yourself, but that's a tiny fraction of what a person actually needs. A state can't just decide it's legal for your back leg or your house and leave everything else in the dark.

I wish the rules would just make sense.

I think of it less like a battery and more like a leaky pipe. Nerve cells have channels in their outer walls that let sodium in. When a signal hits, those channels pop open, and the rush of sodium changes the charge across the cell wall. That's what people call electricity in the body. At least that's how it was explained to me.

What i find interesting is that it doesn't happen everywhere at once. Your back leg isn't constantly sparking. It happens in little waves along a nerve, like a row of dominoes. If a channel gets stuck, the signal can go sideways, and suddenly you're getting that weird twitching. I've seen it happen.

We never got to eat, so I can’t tell you if the food was good. We got there at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, picked this place since we had a 10:00 p.m. show at the same hotel and figured dining would be simple. We put our names on their useless digital waitlist. At 8:23 p.m. we were told to come back to pay. We went back, then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before a staff member casually mentioned we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15 p.m. It was only a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait stretches that far past paying, say so upfront. Our night isn’t wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if that were an option.

I hit the buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m. and there wasn’t a single person in line. For two people we ended up paying about $130, which felt pretty steep. I’d assumed it would be around the price of a steakhouse, but it actually came in slightly more expensive than I expected.

The big letdown was that there was no steak on the menu. For that price, I figured at least a steak option would be there. The meats included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those feel like things you can grab at other Las Vegas buffets for way less.

Seafood had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are all over Vegas buffets, but rock crab claws were something I hadn’t seen anywhere else, so those caught my attention. The only catch was there were no crab crackers. Staff said there were wooden mallets, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing shells and sending pieces flying at them. Ended up just eating the legs.

The Asian station wasn’t especially distinctive. It reminded me of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Desserts included gelato and a few pastries, but nothing jumped out at me. There were fresh juices too, though I didn’t try any.

I’d call the whole thing acceptable but overpriced for what it offers. If there’s no wait, it’s worth trying once. If the line is long, I’d think twice.

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking. I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches (the small bump under your finger, then a soft landing at the bottom). My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard. My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle. Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now. Does that make sense to you?

About two years ago I called Rockmount Ranch Wear and ordered two shirts for my dad. They never showed up because the rep wrote down the address wrong. Her handwritten 7 got read as a 1, so a package meant for 5407 ended up at 5401. The people there took it to the local UPS store to get it sent back, but after that it just vanished. We didn't find out until several weeks had passed.

While the dispute was going on we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount said no refund on the original two, and the owner handled it from there. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address, but no refund until the shirts came back. He even suggested it was partly our fault for not being friendly enough to the folks at 5401, only four doors away. I thought that was a stretch. We disputed the original charge with the card company and got the credit in the end.
